title: Dominic and the Parish
premise: Estate lawyer Bram Fairweather is summoned to the decaying parish of St. Aldwyn to execute a will naming a man who died thirty years ago — a will dated three days after his death. Twin letters, one confessing to the old drowning and one promising 'the rest of the truth,' pull Bram into a tangle of alibis built by four parish families whose children have inherited more than property. As the statute of limitations ticks down, Bram discovers the confessing letter was written by the victim himself, who never drowned but vanished into a new identity. In the end, Bram must choose between exposing the living dead man and protecting the daughter who has finally found belonging in the parish that erased her father.
about_author: Orsen Reyes spent a decade as a probate clerk in coastal England before turning to fiction, and his mysteries are known for their forensic attention to paperwork and inheritance law. He lives in a converted tithe barn with his partner and an archive of unread wills he insists are research.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Arriving at rain-soaked St. Aldwyn, Bram reads a will executed for Thomas Ellery — drowned thirty years ago, yet signed and witnessed after his death. The parishioners close ranks with practiced smiles. Emotional beat: unease curdling into professional obsession as Bram realizes everyone in the churchyard knew the document existed.

chapters.title: Twin Letters
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, intercut with flashbacks to 1994. Two letters surface: one confessing to Ellery's murder, signed by the late sexton; one unsigned, promising 'the rest of the truth' if Bram stops asking questions. The alibis of the four founding families align too perfectly. Emotional beat: dread — someone is watching Bram's investigation from inside the house.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibi
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Digging through parish registers, Bram finds Ellery's drowning was staged by his own family to free him from debts and a doomed marriage — but the confession letter's ink dates prove it was written recently, by someone alive. The statute expires in nine days. Emotional beat: vertigo, as every ally becomes a suspect and Bram's duty to the estate collides with growing love for Ellery's estranged daughter, Maren.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, climax at the flooded quarry on the statute's final night. The confessor is revealed: Ellery himself, alive under a new name, confessing not to murder but to abandoning Maren — and dying now, truly, willing the truth into the open. Bram burns nothing, hides nothing, but frames the record so Maren inherits both the estate and her father's name. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution — justice served as mercy, belonging chosen over duty.
